nodes.name: Large VLMs impractical for resource-constrained environments
nodes.description: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress, yet their large scale often renders them impractical for resource-constrained environments.

nodes.name: Architectural mods and 'think' responses increase inference cost
nodes.description: Architectural changes and the verbose 'think' responses preceding answers can significantly increase inference latency and computational memory requirements.

nodes.name: VLMs impractical for resource-limited devices
nodes.description: These challenges render many powerful VLMs impractical for resource-limited settings like smartphones and augmented reality (AR) devices.

nodes.name: Need for balanced VLM design
nodes.description: There is a growing imperative within the research community to develop VLM designs that achieve a compelling balance between strong vision-language capabilities, low inference latency, and a lightweight model footprint.

nodes.name: RIL introduced to avoid architectural mods and lengthy think responses
nodes.description: RIL is introduced as an approach for developing high-performing, efficient VLMs that avoids architectural modifications and the need for lengthy 'think' responses.

nodes.name: RIL integrates GRPO and GAIL
nodes.description: RIL is an efficient training algorithm integrating principles from both GRPO and the GAIL framework.

nodes.name: RIL central objective
nodes.description: The central objective of RIL is to enable smaller VLMs (e.g., 7B models) to effectively mimic the text generation style of significantly larger VLMs (e.g., 72B models).

nodes.name: Verbalization effect
nodes.description: Prior works have argued that natural language response-based distillation is more effective than high-dimensional feature distillation, emphasizing the importance of utilizing the language head—referred to as the verbalization effect.

nodes.name: Motivation to leverage response similarity
nodes.description: Motivated by the verbalization effect, RIL began by leveraging the similarity in natural language responses between teacher and student models.

nodes.name: LLM-based discriminator introduced
nodes.description: RIL employs an LLM-based discriminator trained to distinguish between the text responses generated by the student (small VLMs) and the teacher (large VLMs).

nodes.name: Discriminator output as similarity reward
nodes.description: The discriminator's output provides a similarity reward signal, guiding the student VLMs, which act as a generator, to produce responses increasingly akin to those of the teacher.

nodes.name: Discriminator architecture mirrors generator
nodes.description: To maintain training stability and prevent the generator or discriminator from overpowering the other (the balance problem), the discriminator's architecture initially mirrors that of the generator.

nodes.name: Continuous discriminator scores introduce ambiguity
nodes.description: Relying on continuous discriminator scores (ranging from zero to one) to assess similarity to large VLM outputs can introduce ambiguity into the learning signal.

nodes.name: Binarized similarity reward
nodes.description: To ensure a clearer and more decisive reward, the discriminator's similarity score is converted into a binary value.

nodes.name: Discriminator lacks factual verification
nodes.description: The discriminator, by design, focuses on stylistic similarity and does not inherently verify factual correctness against ground truth answers, which could otherwise lead to performance degradation.

nodes.name: LLM-as-a-Judge mitigates factual-correctness gap
nodes.description: RIL mitigates the discriminator's lack of factual verification by incorporating an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide a separate binary reward signal based on the accuracy of the generated response.

nodes.name: Limited student knowledge hinders GRPO learning pathways
nodes.description: A challenge arises during the GRPO phase: if the student VLMs, due to their more limited knowledge, fail to generate any correct responses for a given task, they struggle to identify effective learning pathways.

nodes.name: Incorporate both student and teacher responses during GRPO
nodes.description: To provide clearer guidance, RIL incorporates text responses from both student and teacher VLMs during the GRPO training step.

nodes.name: Dual-source GRPO stabilizes training and enables surpassing teachers
nodes.description: This strategy of incorporating both student and teacher responses during GRPO not only stabilizes RIL training but also creates opportunities for the student VLM to potentially surpass the performance of larger teachers.

nodes.name: Multiple teacher VLMs boost performance beyond single teacher
nodes.description: Sourcing text responses from multiple large teacher VLMs significantly boosts student performance beyond what a single teacher can achieve, owing to the richer diversity of responses and the consequently more robust discriminator.

nodes.name: Multi-source GRPO gives clearer exemplars
nodes.description: This enriched learning environment is further enhanced during the GRPO step: by incorporating text responses from both student and teacher VLMs, the student is provided with clearer exemplars for reaching correct answers.

nodes.name: RIL synergy with distillation-based VLMs
nodes.description: RIL demonstrates particular synergy with distillation-based VLMs; these models show marked performance improvements because their inherent feature alignment through distillation complements RIL's objectives.

nodes.name: RIL preserves inference speed
nodes.description: A crucial practical advantage of RIL is its inference efficiency: trained models do not require an explicit 'think' phase before generating answers, thereby maintaining the same inference speed as the original student VLM.

nodes.name: Table 2: multi-teacher outperforms single teacher on MathVista
nodes.description: Table 2 shows that for Qwen2.5-VL-7B, using both Qwen2.5-VL-72B and InternVL3-78B as teachers yields a MathVista score of 79.7, versus 74.5 with Qwen2.5-VL-72B alone and 74.6 with InternVL3-78B alone.

nodes.name: LLM-as-a-Judge substantially advantages applicability
nodes.description: RIL's reliance on LLM-as-a-Judge for accuracy evaluation offers substantial advantages in applicability.

nodes.name: Conventional parsing limited to predefined-metric domains
nodes.description: Unlike methods such as DeepSeek-R1 and its variants, which often use conventional answer parsing for reward computation, RIL is not limited to domains with predefined metrics (e.g., math or image grounding).

nodes.name: Parsing struggles with open-ended visual questions
nodes.description: Conventional parsing struggles with open-ended general visual questions, such as 'How to cook this dish?' based on a food image, or 'Summarize this movie' from its poster.

nodes.name: Parsing cannot flexibly compare differently formatted answers
nodes.description: Parsing poses a challenge to flexibly compare different types of answers, e.g., if a response is 'The answer is twenty percent' but its ground truth is '20'.

nodes.name: LLM-as-a-Judge enables broad VQA applicability
nodes.description: The versatile evaluation power of LLM-as-a-Judge enables RIL's successful application to a broad spectrum of visual question answering tasks, fostering strong performance in recognition, OCR, common-sense reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and chart/document understanding.

nodes.name: GAIL as foundational IL framework
nodes.description: Generative adversarial imitation learning (GAIL) is a foundational framework in imitation learning, employing a generator (e.g., small student VLMs) that attempts to replicate expert behavior (e.g., large teacher VLMs) by producing indistinguishable outputs, while a discriminator distinguishes generator from expert.

nodes.name: GAIL frames IL as minimax game without explicit reward
nodes.description: By framing imitation learning as a minimax game, GAIL leverages adversarial training to align the behavior of the generator with that of the expert without explicitly defining a reward function, relying only on discriminator scores.

nodes.name: RIL's four key modifications to GAIL/GRPO
nodes.description: Based on GAIL's effectiveness, RIL integrates reinforcement and imitation learning for VLMs with four key modifications: (1) combining GRPO and GAIL with explicit reward design, (2) binarizing the discriminator's output scores to stabilize training, (3) incorporating LLM-as-a-Judge to evaluate answer rewards, and (4) utilizing teacher-generated text responses during GRPO updates as direct guidance.

nodes.name: Four modifications stabilize training and enable surpassing teachers
nodes.description: These four modifications not only stabilize RIL training but also provide a mechanism for student VLMs to potentially exceed the performance of teacher VLMs.

nodes.name: RIL maintains inference speed and tokenizer independence
nodes.description: RIL does not require an explicit think-answer process, thereby maintaining the same inference speed, and it is independent of any particular image embedding methods or language tokenizers used in the student or teacher VLMs.

nodes.name: Discriminator pre-training is crucial
nodes.description: With the student (small) VLMs serving as the generator, the effective pre-training of the discriminator is crucial; without adequate pre-training, it would yield unreliable scores, undermining its utility and potentially degrading overall model performance.

nodes.name: Response dataset collection for pre-training
nodes.description: To prepare for pre-training, N text responses are generated for each given question from both the student VLMs and the teacher VLMs, forming a dataset used to train the discriminator.

nodes.name: Discriminator maximization objective (Eq. 1)
nodes.description: The discriminator Dφ is trained to maximize an objective that pushes it to output a score approaching one for student responses and zero for teacher responses.

nodes.name: Discriminator head replaces language head
nodes.description: To elicit the scalar discrimination score, the standard language head of the VLM is replaced with a linear discriminator head, computing the score via sigmoid on the final sequence token's representation.

nodes.name: SFT warm-up precedes RIL loop
nodes.description: The RIL process commences after an initial supervised finetuning (SFT) phase for the student VLMs, acting as a crucial warm-up that acclimates the student to the target data distribution.

nodes.name: Combined 2G response set per question
nodes.description: For each question in a training batch, G responses are generated from the current student VLMs and G responses are retrieved from teacher VLMs, yielding a combined set of 2G responses.

nodes.name: Discriminator updated each RIL iteration
nodes.description: Within each RIL iteration, the discriminator is first updated on the 2G responses, ensuring it maintains its ability to distinguish student from teacher outputs as the student VLMs evolve.

nodes.name: Student updated via Dr.GRPO objective
nodes.description: The student VLMs are then updated using an objective derived from Dr.GRPO, an advanced variant of GRPO that provides unbiased advantage estimates.

nodes.name: Composite reward: similarity + answer
nodes.description: The total reward for each response is a composite signal comprising two binary components: a similarity reward (based on the discriminator score being below 0.5) and an answer reward (factual correctness via LLM-as-a-Judge).

nodes.name: Answer reward essential for factual accuracy
nodes.description: The inclusion of the answer reward is essential, as the discriminator alone primarily captures stylistic similarity and does not guarantee factual accuracy, the absence of which could lead to significant performance issues.

nodes.name: RL-only ablation baselines (GRPO/Dr.GRPO)
nodes.description: RL agents trained solely with GRPO or its advanced variant Dr.GRPO, without the discriminator or associated similarity rewards, are evaluated as baselines to isolate RIL's component contributions.

nodes.name: RIL outperforms RL-only approaches (Table 1)
nodes.description: As shown in Table 1, RIL, which integrates reinforcement and imitation learning elements based on Dr.GRPO and GAIL, demonstrably outperforms RL-only approaches, confirming the efficacy of the unified training algorithm.

nodes.name: Table 1: Qwen2.5-VL-7B MathVista gains
nodes.description: Table 1 shows RIL (Dr.GRPO + GAIL) raises Qwen2.5-VL-7B's MathVista score from 67.8 (base) to 74.5, compared to 69.5 with RL (Dr.GRPO) alone.

nodes.name: RIL narrows gap to and surpasses SOTA VLMs
nodes.description: RIL-trained student VLMs exhibit highly competitive performance against a range of recent open-source and closed-source models, substantially narrowing the performance gap to state-of-the-art VLMs and, in several instances, surpassing them.

nodes.name: Increasing update iterations µ degrades performance
nodes.description: Table 5(a) shows that a single update iteration (µ=1) for both discriminator and student VLMs is sufficient for strong performance, and balanced accuracy decreases monotonically as µ increases from 1 to 12.

nodes.name: More student-update iterations risk overfitting
nodes.description: More update iterations, especially for student VLM updates, can risk overfitting.

nodes.name: KL penalty coefficient β trade-off examined
nodes.description: The impact of the KL-divergence penalty coefficient β on RIL performance is examined in Table 5(b).

nodes.name: Constraining updates is crucial but overly restrictive β hinders performance
nodes.description: Results confirm that while constraining policy updates is crucial for stability, an overly restrictive penalty (large β) can hinder performance.

nodes.name: Module-update importance examined (Table 5c)
nodes.description: Table 5(c) details the importance of updating different parameter groups within the student VLMs during RIL.

nodes.name: Self-attention, word-embeddings, language head matter most
nodes.description: Training the self-attention layers, word embeddings, and the language head yields more significant gains than updating feed-forward networks (FFN) or layer normalization parameters.

nodes.name: Necessity of continuously updating discriminator investigated
nodes.description: Table 5(d) investigates the necessity of continuously updating the discriminator during RIL training.

nodes.name: Fixed pre-trained discriminator beats RL-only but trails continuous update
nodes.description: A fixed (not updated) pre-trained discriminator can outperform RL-only baselines, but overall RIL efficacy still critically depends on leveraging a continuously trained discriminator during RIL.

nodes.name: Table 5(d) MathVista scores: none < fixed < continuous
nodes.description: For Qwen2.5-VL-7B on MathVista, no discriminator scores 69.5, a fixed pre-trained discriminator scores 75.3, and a continuously updated discriminator scores 79.7.

nodes.name: Replacing LLM-as-a-Judge with parsing degrades performance
nodes.description: Table 5(e) shows that replacing LLM-as-a-Judge for answer rewards with conventional answer parsing significantly degrades performance, particularly on general visual questions where fixed parsing rules are inadequate.

nodes.name: Flexible LLM-based evaluation is needed
nodes.description: This highlights the need for flexible, LLM-based evaluation of answer correctness.

nodes.name: SFT beneficial but RIL delivers larger subsequent gains
nodes.description: Table 5(e) also affirms that while initial SFT is beneficial for capturing the training data distribution, RIL subsequently delivers substantially larger improvements.

nodes.name: RIL evaluated on distillation-trained student VLMs (Table 5f)
nodes.description: RIL's effectiveness is examined on student VLMs already trained on distillation methods like MiniLLM, DistilLLM, LLaVA-KD, and VLsI.

nodes.name: RIL more potent for distillation-based VLMs
nodes.description: RIL proves particularly potent for distillation-trained models compared to non-distillation counterparts, likely because prior feature alignment through distillation primes them for RIL's alignment mechanisms.

nodes.name: Binary similarity reward enables efficient, stable training
nodes.description: The binary similarity reward introduced in Sec. 3.3 enables more efficient and stable training of RIL.

nodes.name: Binary reward outperforms continuous/multi-level discretization
nodes.description: As shown in Fig. 6, the binary reward consistently outperforms continuous and multi-level discretizations, suggesting that binary feedback provides clearer and more reliable learning signals.

nodes.name: Models struggle to interpret subtle continuous reward differences
nodes.description: This improvement arises because models often struggle to interpret subtle differences in continuous rewards (e.g., why a score of 0.21 should be preferred over 0.20).

nodes.name: Teacher VLMs produce more diverse/higher-quality responses than SFT ground truth
nodes.description: RIL leverages the diversity of responses generated by large VLMs, which tend to produce more varied and higher-quality answers beyond the ground truth answers used in SFT training datasets.

nodes.name: More teacher-generated responses improve student performance
nodes.description: As illustrated in Fig. 7, increasing the number of teacher-generated responses consistently improves the student model's performance, demonstrating that richer supervision from diverse teacher outputs enhances the student VLM's overall generalization ability.

nodes.name: RIL guides students beyond fixed ground truth
nodes.description: RIL exploits diverse, high-quality teacher responses to guide smaller VLMs toward learning more flexible responses beyond fixed ground truth answers.

nodes.name: RIL operates on text, not high-dimensional logits
nodes.description: Unlike conventional distillation, which typically requires student VLMs to replicate the high-dimensional logit features of teacher models, RIL operates exclusively on generated text responses in natural language.

nodes.name: Text-only operation liberates RIL from feature-level constraints
nodes.description: This fundamental difference liberates RIL from restrictive feature-level constraints, such as the need for identical image embedding strategies or perfectly aligned language tokenizers between student and teacher VLMs.

nodes.name: Trainable discriminator vs static KL divergence
nodes.description: Common distillation methods often rely on KL divergence—a static, non-trainable metric devoid of contextual understanding—but RIL employs a trainable discriminator which assesses natural language responses directly, learning to discern nuanced similarities and stylistic differences.

nodes.name: Trainable discriminator makes RIL flexible and powerful
nodes.description: The adaptability of the trainable discriminator in capturing contextual relationships makes RIL a particularly flexible and powerful approach for lightweight VLM enhancement.

nodes.name: RIL currently focused on post-instruction-tuning alignment
nodes.description: While RIL demonstrates significant strengths, its current implementation has been focused primarily on the post-instruction tuning alignment phase.

nodes.name: Future work: extend discriminator to instruction-tuning stage
nodes.description: A promising avenue for future research involves extending the utility of the discriminator to the initial visual instruction tuning stage itself, hypothesizing it could offer benefits for more efficient instruction following from the outset.

isolated_nodes.name: AGI pursuit driven by instruction-tuned LLMs
isolated_nodes.description: The pursuit of artificial general intelligence (AGI) has gained momentum, with much of the initial progress driven by instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs).

isolated_nodes.name: VLMs extend LLMs to multimodal understanding
isolated_nodes.description: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) represent a significant step forward, extending the LLM framework to integrate visual data and thereby achieve multimodal understanding.

isolated_nodes.name: Historical scaling strategies for VLMs
isolated_nodes.description: Historically, enhancements in vision-language performance have primarily relied on traditional strategies such as scaling up model sizes and expanding visual instruction tuning datasets.

isolated_nodes.name: Architectural modification approaches to VLMs
isolated_nodes.description: More recent advancements have explored architectural modifications, such as directly altering model structures or integrating auxiliary vision and reasoning modules.

isolated_nodes.name: Think-answer paradigm following DeepSeek-R1
isolated_nodes.description: The 'think-answer' paradigm has gained prominence following DeepSeek-R1's application of reinforcement learning (RL) via GRPO.

isolated_nodes.name: Student model choices
isolated_nodes.description: RIL's student models are recently released architectures such as Qwen2.5-VL (3B and 7B variants) and InternVL3 (1B, 2B, and 8B variants).

isolated_nodes.name: Teacher model choices
isolated_nodes.description: RIL's teacher models are Qwen2.5-VL-72B and InternVL3-78B, selected for strong performance on benchmarks like the VLM Leaderboard.

isolated_nodes.name: LLM-as-a-Judge model choice
isolated_nodes.description: RIL uses Qwen2.5-32B as the LLM-as-a-Judge, following the methodology of Zheng et al., and this model is not trained itself.

isolated_nodes.name: Closed-source VLM competitors
isolated_nodes.description: RIL aims to develop efficient, high-performing VLMs capable of rivaling leading closed-source systems like GPT-4o, Gemini, and Claude-3.5 Sonnet.

isolated_nodes.name: Discriminator prompt format
isolated_nodes.description: Figure 3 shows the discriminator is given a system prompt instructing it to return 0 if a response was generated by the teacher model and 1 if generated by the student model.

isolated_nodes.name: LLM-as-a-Judge prompt format
isolated_nodes.description: Figure 4 shows the LLM-as-a-Judge is given a question, ground truth, and generated text, and outputs an evaluation score of 0 or 1 wrapped in answer tags after a brief explanation.

isolated_nodes.name: Table 3: RIL vs standard/smaller open-source VLMs
isolated_nodes.description: Table 3 compares RIL-applied VLMs against standard or smaller model size open-source VLMs, showing RIL-trained variants outperforming their non-RIL counterparts and many peer models across benchmarks.

isolated_nodes.name: Table 4: RIL vs large open- and closed-source VLMs
isolated_nodes.description: Table 4 compares RIL-applied 7B/8B VLMs against much larger (72B+) open-source and closed-source VLMs, showing RIL-trained small models achieving competitive or superior scores on several benchmarks such as ChartQA and MM-Vet.

isolated_nodes.name: Figure 5: similarity and answer rewards increase over training
isolated_nodes.description: Figure 5 illustrates that over the course of RIL training, similarity rewards (from the discriminator) and answer rewards (from LLM-as-a-Judge) both increase alongside overall average benchmark performance.

isolated_nodes.name: Discriminator pre-training compute cost
isolated_nodes.description: Using 256 NVIDIA A100 GPUs, pre-training the discriminator on 1.2M samples (40K samples × 16 generated responses × 2 for teacher and student) takes approximately 1 to 3 days.

isolated_nodes.name: SFT compute cost
isolated_nodes.description: The SFT step on the 4M-sample SFT dataset takes around 3 to 5 days.

isolated_nodes.name: RIL loop compute cost
isolated_nodes.description: Conducting the RIL loop for the sampled 40K data requires an additional 3 to 5 days using 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs.

isolated_nodes.name: Clipping hyperparameter fixed at 0.2
isolated_nodes.description: For the optimization objective of student VLMs, the clipping hyperparameter ε is consistently set to 0.2 across hyperparameter analyses.

isolated_nodes.name: vLLM used for fast text generation
isolated_nodes.description: Training and evaluation are conducted mainly on NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs, using vLLM built on PagedAttention for fast text generation during training.

isolated_nodes.name: DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 and AdamW used for training
isolated_nodes.description: The DeepSpeed engine with ZeRO-3 and the AdamW optimizer are used, applying a linearly decayed learning rate from 1e-5 to 1e-6 for pre-training the discriminator and SFT of student VLMs.

isolated_nodes.name: Mimicking-step generation hyperparameters
isolated_nodes.description: The mimicking step requires a static learning rate of 1e-6 and µ=1 iteration to train both student VLMs and the discriminator, generating G=4 responses per question with temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95, top-k 50, and repetition penalty 1.05.

isolated_nodes.name: RIL's increased computational cost vs GRPO
isolated_nodes.description: Compared to GRPO, RIL requires increased computational costs during training due to teacher, student, discriminator, and LLM-as-a-Judge components.

isolated_nodes.name: CPU/GPU weight offloading mitigates RIL cost
isolated_nodes.description: Discriminator and student training costs during the RIL loop are mitigated by offloading model weights to the CPU when not in use and loading them to the GPU via the DeepSpeed API, feasible because discriminator and student share the same architecture.

isolated_nodes.name: 4M-sample visual instruction tuning dataset
isolated_nodes.description: A 4M-sample visual instruction tuning dataset is assembled encompassing diverse vision-language tasks including VQA, captioning, chart/diagram/document understanding, common-sense knowledge, and scientific/mathematical problem-solving.

isolated_nodes.name: 40K-sample RIL dataset curation method
isolated_nodes.description: A 40K-sample dataset is curated for RIL from the full instruction-tuning dataset based on log-probability sampling and overlong filtering.

isolated_nodes.name: RIL democratizes lightweight VLM deployment
isolated_nodes.description: RIL democratizes access to advanced vision-language capabilities by enabling lightweight, efficient models to run on edge devices and in low-resource settings, thereby lowering deployment costs and environmental impact.

isolated_nodes.name: RIL fosters interoperability across architectures
isolated_nodes.description: RIL fosters seamless interoperability across diverse model architectures and tokenization schemes.

isolated_nodes.name: Table 1 benchmark suite
isolated_nodes.description: Table 1 compares performances using answer rewards from LLM-as-a-Judge with purely RL on GRPO and Dr.GRPO, versus RIL using similarity and answer rewards from GAIL, across 14 benchmarks: AI2D, ChartQA, MathVista, MMB/MMBCN, MM-Vet, MM-Vet-v2, MMMU, MMMU-Pro, MMStar, BLINK, SEED, SEED2+, and RealWorldQA.

isolated_nodes.name: Discriminator objective formula (Eq. 1)
isolated_nodes.description: The discriminator's training objective is mathematically expressed as maximizing the average of log Dφ(q, student response) plus log(1 − Dφ(q, teacher response)) over N sample pairs.

isolated_nodes.name: Dr.GRPO advantage estimate formula (Eq. 2)
isolated_nodes.description: The Dr.GRPO-derived objective computes the advantage for each response as its reward minus the mean reward across all 2G sampled responses for that question.

isolated_nodes.name: GAIL's minimax alignment without explicit reward
isolated_nodes.description: GAIL leverages adversarial training to align generator behavior with expert behavior without explicitly defining a reward function, relying only on discriminator scores.

structural_reasoning: This graph decomposes the RIL paper into 21 small-to-medium connected components, each capturing a tight chain of motivation, mechanism, or evidence (e.g., C1 traces the motivation-to-RIL-objective chain; C10 traces the full per-iteration RIL training loop; C11 and C15-C18 capture the main ablation and headline-result findings). Components are kept small and strictly evidence-linked because the source text presents most claims as sequential, single-directional argumentation (motivation → design choice → mechanism → result) rather than densely cross-referenced propositions, so few edges naturally bridge across these thematic clusters (e.g., multi-teacher benefit in C6 versus the discriminator-training loop in C9-C10 are discussed in adjacent but not explicitly cross-referenced passages). Node/edge scores are high (9-10) throughout since almost every edge is a direct restatement of a stated cause-effect or challenge-solution relationship within a single sentence or adjacent sentence pair; the two 9.0 edge-score components (C6, C18, C20) reflect slightly more interpretive links (e.g., connecting the qualitative multi-teacher claim to the quantitative Table 2 result, or connecting two independently-justified benefits of the trainable discriminator) where the paper does not explicitly state the connective relationship but strongly implies it through proximity and shared subject. A substantial isolated_nodes set (background/related-work claims, prompt templates, table/figure summaries, and compute/appendix details) is retained separately because these are self-contained factual statements without argued dependencies on other propositions in the paper.
